# The Weight of What He Witnessed

Kofi is a 59-year-old Ghanaian-born professor of comparative literature at a mid-sized university, a man whose life has been built around language — around finding the precise words to illuminate human experience. These days, he finds himself unable to speak about the thing that matters most.

Three years ago, Kofi watched his younger brother, Emmanuel, be struck by a vehicle while the two of them were crossing a busy intersection near Kofi's apartment. They had been arguing, lightly, about nothing — a football match, a family obligation — and then Emmanuel stepped forward a half-second before the light changed. Kofi was close enough to feel the displacement of air. He held his brother on the pavement while strangers gathered and called for help, watching Emmanuel's face change in ways he cannot bring himself to describe, even now. Emmanuel survived, but sustained a severe traumatic brain injury. He lives in a care facility in Accra, largely unresponsive, no longer the man Kofi grew up with. Kofi has visited twice. Each time, he left earlier than he planned.

In the months following the accident, Kofi told himself he was managing. He returned to teaching within two weeks, because standing in front of students felt like the only thing that still made structural sense. He graded papers. He attended faculty meetings. He cooked meals he didn't eat. But the intersection found ways to follow him. He began taking elaborate detours to avoid it, then avoiding the entire neighborhood, and eventually restructuring his commute so completely that what once took fifteen minutes now takes nearly an hour. He tells colleagues it's for the exercise.

Sleep has become a negotiation he rarely wins. He lies down and his mind returns, with cinematic precision, to the sound of the impact, to the particular quality of Emmanuel's breathing in those first minutes on the ground. He wakes at 3 or 4 in the morning, heart hammering, and sits at his desk reading until dawn — not because reading soothes him, but because it gives his vigilance somewhere to go. He has read more in the past three years than in the decade before, and retained almost none of it.

In the classroom, Kofi is still formidable — his students describe him as exacting, brilliant, occasionally remote. What they don't see is how often he loses the thread mid-lecture when a text touches on themes of sudden loss or bodily harm. Last semester, teaching Achebe, he stopped mid-sentence and stood at the whiteboard for a long moment before dismissing the class early, claiming a scheduling conflict. He has begun avoiding certain texts he once loved.

He carries a particular and corrosive guilt. He knows, rationally, that he did not cause the accident. He has told himself this many times, in many formulations. But he also knows that they were arguing, that he had said something sharp just before the light changed, and that Emmanuel turned toward him — perhaps to respond — in the moment before stepping off the curb. This detail has become a splinter he cannot leave alone. He replays the sequence, adjusting variables, searching for the version where he stays quiet, where he reaches out and grabs his brother's arm, where everything is different.

Kofi has not told his family the full shape of what he carries. He is the eldest son, the one who left for graduate school in England at twenty-two and built a life abroad. He has always been the capable one. He calls his mother in Accra every Sunday and speaks warmly about his week, describing a life that is, in most of its surface details, intact. He is a man who has spent his career teaching others how stories mean something. He has not yet found a way to tell this one.
